content: It is essential to establish the scope of treatments that can be delivered without compromising quality. Such evaluations must be objective and evidence-based, rather than relying solely on user opinions, as individuals in remote areas may have limited knowledge of what to expect from services and may hold low expectations regarding the fit, function, and comfort of assistive devices. Mobile Prosthetics and Orthotics Services Mobile prosthetics and orthotics services are typically a temporary solution aimed at raising awareness of needs, improving access to services, and laying the groundwork for a decentralized network of secondary-level service units. In some countries, mobile services are the only viable way to reach populations dispersed across vast, hard-to-access areas such as deserts, islands, and mountainous regions. These services are a critical component of the service delivery system and may be indispensable for ensuring that all individuals in need receive appropriate care. Example: Mobile Prosthetics and Orthotics Services in Brazil In 2008, the São Paulo State Government in Brazil initiated a network of 20 permanent rehabilitation facilities. While these facilities were being constructed, equipped, and staffed, a mobile unit was introduced in 2009 to provide decentralized services, build the capacity of local professionals, raise awareness about the rights of people with disabilities to access appropriate services, and collect data on service needs. This mobile unit operated until 2011 and consisted of a 5-meter-wide tractor-trailer equipped with rooms for waiting, consultation, therapy, fitting, assembly, machine work, plaster work, and administrative support. Staff included prosthetics and orthotics personnel, doctors, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, nurses, administrative officers, and a bioengineer. The unit provided services in nine of the state’s 17 regional health departments, delivering over 3,300 assistive products, including lowerand upper-limb orthoses and prostheses, shoes, insoles, canes, crutches, and walking frames, benefiting approximately 1,800 users. The mobile service also facilitated the establishment of new permanent rehabilitation facilities in previously underserved regions. Outreach Services In exceptional circumstances, such as emergencies or to reach very remote populations, prosthetics and orthotics units can organize outreach services. These typically involve a series of visits to a location, often in collaboration with district or sub-district hospitals or primary healthcare centers. Outreach services are delivered by a multidisciplinary team similar to that of a mobile unit but without most of the tools and machines. Follow-up can be conducted by community workers or through additional visits. Example: Outreach Prosthetics and Orthotics Services in Nepal Nepal, with a population of 27 million spread across diverse geographic regions, faces challenges in providing access to prosthetics and orthotics services, particularly in the Hill and Mountain regions. Outreach services are essential for reaching underserved areas, often requiring 10–15 hours of travel to reach a district, with 1–2 days spent at each site. Potential users are referred by village leaders and local health, social, and education personnel. The outreach team provides on-site assessments and rehabilitation services, including prefabricated orthoses and mobility aids. Custom-built products are delivered during follow-up visits, though most users requiring extensive treatment are referred to service facilities. Integration with Community-Based Rehabilitation (CBR) and Other Programs Prosthetics and orthotics services can collaborate with community programs, such as CBR initiatives, to identify and refer individuals in need of assistive devices and to provide follow-up care. CBR workers can conduct basic functional assessments, provide simple rehabilitation treatments, train family members, and facilitate referrals to specialized services. Advances in information and communication technology, such as telemedicine and telerehabilitation, can further enhance service delivery by improving access to specialized assessments and follow-up care. Example: Telemedicine and Telerehabilitation in the Philippines In the Philippines, the Department of Rehabilitation Medicine at the Philippine General Hospital implemented the Amputee Screening through Cellphone Networking (ASCENT) program. This initiative uses mobile phones to record medical histories, capture images and videos, and transmit data to a centralized database. ASCENT has created a registry of amputees, facilitated screening for prosthesis use, and identified individuals at risk of secondary amputation. The program has also supported the development of a prostheses benefit package under the Philippine Health Insurance Commission. Maintenance and Repair Services For prostheses and orthoses to remain functional and comfortable, regular maintenance and occasional repairs are necessary. Adjustments may be required due to changes in the user’s physical condition, such as muscle atrophy or weight gain. Maintenance and repair services should be an integral part of the prosthetics and orthotics service system and should be provided as close to users as possible. Decentralized facilities and trained community workers can play a role in delivering these services, which are critical for ensuring user satisfaction and reducing long-term costs. Service Provision in Disasters Prosthetics and orthotics services are often needed following natural or man-made disasters, such as earthquakes or conflicts, which result in an increased number of individuals with acquired impairments. In the emergency phase, services must be planned promptly, with data collection on the number of victims, local service capacity, and required resources. During the reconstruction phase, fitting of prostheses and orthoses should begin as soon as injuries heal and security conditions permit. Inclusive and Exclusive Service Units Prosthetics and orthotics service units may operate as exclusive, stand-alone entities or as integrated components of larger health or rehabilitation facilities. Integrated units, often located within hospitals, facilitate collaboration with other healthcare providers and improve service outcomes. In some cases, service units may specialize in specific areas, such as spinal orthoses, though it is generally more practical and cost-effective to provide a full range of services in one location. Example: Integrated Mobility Device Services in Samoa The Samoa Integrated Mobility Device Services program combines various assistive technologies, including prosthetics and orthotics, into a single service unit. A new facility staffed by trained personnel has been established to provide consistent and reliable services. Equipment and Safety Prosthetics and orthotics service units require specialized tools and equipment for the fabrication and fitting of devices. Investing in high-quality equipment, even if initially more expensive, can reduce maintenance and replacement costs in the long term.
